title: Trump Ties Saudi Nuclear Deal to Israel Recognition, Raising Stakes in the Middle East
summary: In a move that intertwines energy, diplomacy, and Middle Eastern politics, President Donald Trump declared on Thursday that a newly announced U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation deal is contingent on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel. The condition, posted on Truth Social, demands that Riyadh join the Abraham Accords—a series of agreements brokered during Trump's first term that established diplomatic ties between Israel and several Arab nations. "The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!)... is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords," Trump wrote. The White House confirmed that Trump had previously discussed this linkage with Saudi leaders. The deal, unveiled Wednesday by the U.S. Department of Energy, includes a "peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement" and a "bilateral safeguards agreement," which officials say will create a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership while upholding nuclear nonproliferation standards. Yet the announcement has drawn sharp criticism from nonproliferation experts and lawmakers in both parties, who fear that introducing nuclear technology into the volatile region could spark a dangerous arms race. Saudi Arabia has not officially responded to Trump's remarks. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman stated in 2018 that the kingdom would seek nuclear weapons only if Iran developed them—a scenario that has grown more concerning amid ongoing U.S.-Israeli tensions with Iran over its nuclear ambitions. Israel, widely believed to possess nuclear weapons itself, has cautiously welcomed the condition. Economy Minister Nir Barkat said Israel "can manage it" if Saudi Arabia's program remains peaceful, but former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman warned, "Every military nuclear program begins with a civilian one." The Abraham Accords, initially signed by the UAE and Bahrain in 2020 and later joined by Sudan, Morocco, and Kazakhstan, represent a historic shift in Arab-Israeli relations. Trump's latest demand places Saudi Arabia—a regional heavyweight—at the center of this diplomatic puzzle, potentially reshaping alliances ahead of a tense election season in Israel.
why_it_matters: This deal could either stabilize the Middle East or start a nuclear arms race that would threaten global safety and affect future travel, trade, and even energy prices.

background_read: The Abraham Accords, brokered by the U.S. in 2020, were a diplomatic breakthrough that led the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Sudan, Morocco, and later Kazakhstan to establish formal relations with Israel.

President Donald Trump, who began his second term in January 2025, made these accords a signature achievement of his first presidency and is now trying to bring Saudi Arabia — the most influential Arab state — into the fold.

Saudi Arabia and Iran have long been rivals for power in the Middle East; Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS, the kingdom's de facto ruler) once said Saudi Arabia would only pursue a nuclear bomb if Iran got one first.
This linkage comes at a time when Iran is enriching uranium to near weapons-grade levels, raising global concerns about a nuclear arms race in the volatile region.

perspectives.description: The United States and Saudi Arabia secure a major energy partnership worth billions of dollars. Normalizing relations with Israel could open new trade routes and strengthen diplomatic ties in the region, potentially isolating Iran.

Arms control advocates warn that even a peaceful nuclear program can pave the way for weapons. In a neighborhood already full of tensions, this risks triggering an arms race that could spiral out of control, making the Middle East far more dangerous.

The move fits a long American pattern of using economic deals as leverage for diplomatic breakthroughs. However, nuclear agreements have often proved fragile — technology transfers can outlast political goodwill, and inspections can be hard to enforce if trust breaks down.

If Saudi Arabia agrees, the next steps will involve intense negotiations over inspection rights and enrichment limits. If it refuses, the deal collapses and the U.S. may deepen ties with other partners like the UAE, while Saudi Arabia could turn to China or Russia for nuclear technology instead.
